There can be little doubt that the
condition of the Soviet Unions domestic
economy is far from satisfactory The
latest indication Of that Is the Kremlin's
announcement that the State Planning
Commission has been split into two sepa-
rate and distinct agencies-one given the
task of working out programs for future
industrial development, and the other
charged with the responsibility of trying
to solve current production problems.


In connection with this significant
organizational change, Premier Bulganin
has delivered speech plainly suggesting
that the situation calls for urgent meas
ures in both short-range and long-range
sense. According to his exhortations Wig
orouS action must be taken in the indus
trial field to achieve much greater admin
istrative efficiency, lower management
costs, better utilization of present equip
ment, improved factory techniques, faster
and far more extensive chronological prog
ress, and numerous other advances aimed
at bringing about sharp increase in the
Russian workers output per manhour-
thing which now seems exceedingly
deficient by Western standards.


It is true, of course, that the Soviet
Union, by concentrating on the develop
ment and expansion of heavy industry
primarily for military purposes), has
made big gains. Actually and potentially,
however 1t still lags far behind the West
ern world-particularly the United States
and most experts are agreed that our
current wide margin of economic supe-
riority can be maintained and probably
even increased through the remainder of
the century. Meanwhile, as long as the
Kremlin insists upon producing guns be-
fore butter, the people of the USSR will
continue to suffer from a serious lack of
consumer goods And that lack, in turn,
must adversely affect national morale and
initiate against efforts to get more eff
cheney and output from the Russian
worker. After ALL If civilian commodities
are going to remain as scarce as ever for
him, what real incentive has he to do
better job?


Further, apart from the problems thus
entailed in subordinating light industry
to heavy industry the Kremlin is faced
with what has all the earmarks of crit
ical agricultural situation. The Soviet
population has increased enormously, but
the country has less grain per person to-
day than in 1926. And even more strik-
ing-indeed, astonishing-is the fact that
there are now fewer head of cattle in Rus
sia than in the pre-1918 days of the car
DOM Clearly, in nation whose numbers
are growing at rate of million annually,
these statistics can only mean that the
great bulk of the people must live on very
short rationS-a bleak diet hardly condu-
Give to mass contentment.


Although the implications of all this
can be exaggerated, it may we'll be that
the Soviet Unions industrial and agricul-
tural stresses and strains are far more
serious than outsiders have suspected
heretofore. At any rate, the possibility
seems real enough to be reckoned with as
the factor that may be chiefly responsible
for the Kremlin's current effort-a con-
ceivably sincere effort-to ease interna-
tional tensions and seek some sort of
modus vivendi with the West.

A Negro couple has decided
not to occupy a home they were
buying in an all-white neighbor-
hood in Alexandria after shot
gun blast was fired through the
window of the empty house.


Alexandria police, who are In
vestigating the shooting, said
the couple, a captain in the Army
Nurse Corps and her husband,
had moved some furniture into
the two-story brick row house
at 312 Buchanan street before
the shooting occurred last Satur-
day night but were not living in
the house. The blast shattered a
front window.


Police said they did not know
of the shooting until Monday.
when it was reported by the
woman who formerly lived there.


According to police, the Negro
couple decided not to move in
when they learned they would
be the first colored people in
the block and that white neigh
bors were hostile. The nearest
colored residences are about
three blocks away.


A day after the shooting a
note was found tackled to ale
door which stated that colored
people were not welcome in the
neighborhood. The note was
signed 1.-The Confederate CAL
vary" The note was poorly
spelled. and police said it looked
like the incident might be the
work of children.


Police identified the woman
who was selling the house as
Mrs. Florence Guthridge. !

Despite the widespread vio-

Only one incident of violence

Meanwhile, most of the large
cities in both Morocco and AL
geria were silent under a tight
curfew.


Algeria's big seaport of Phil
ippeville, near Constantine, was
under a virtual state of siege.
Police and troops in armored
cars patrolled other Algerian
cities.


In Morocco the fighting con-
tinued mainly in the hills and
the approaches to the Atlas
Mountains.


Severed communications de-
layed casualty reports from many
areas, but those that did trickle
through told a grim tale.


In Algeria, the well-co-ordi-
mated strikes resembled the hit
and-run warfare which laid
waste to French Indo-C China. The
rebels smashed military outposts,
then fed. But the French fought
back effectively.


Like Mau Mau Massacre


In Morocco, some raids were
ominously similar to the Mau
Mau massacres which have
ripped Britain's Kenya Colony.


Worst hit was the little Mo-
roccan mining town of Qued
Fem. about 100 miles southeast
of Casablanca. There 1000 sup
posedly friendly Berber tribes
men poured down from the hills.
shooting, burning and mutilating
non. women and children.


The outbreak at Oued Fem
was only one Of many. French

LONDON. July 13 P.-Ruth
Ellis, beautiful blond mother of
two children. died on the GAL
lows inAondon's Holloway Prison
for Women today for the Easter
Sunday murder of the lover who
tilted her.


The 28-year-old divorce, a
former model and night club
hostess, was the 14th woman to
be hanged in Britain this CEN
tury and the third since World
War II. Her sentencing revived
q Nationwide controversy over
capital punishment, which con-
tinued unabated today.


A crowd of 1000 persons
some weeping, others laughing
stood in the grimy North Lon
don. street outside the iyy-cov-
cred, red-brick prison as Hang
man Albert Pierrepoint pulled
the death trap.


Sobs Self to Sleep


Reports from inside the prison
said the icy calm that Mrs. Ellis
had maintained during her trial
in June and ever since finally
broke last night. Prison sources
said she sobbed herself to sleep,
screaming, II don't want to die. ~


The matrons let her sleep
until the last minute, foregoing
the usual $50 waking hour.


Earlier in the night she had
said goodby to her mother and
father. who reported she was re-
signed to her fate. The woman
had refused to appeal for mercy
Home Secretary Gwilym Lloyd
George. the only man who can
recommend royal clemency.
earlier this week turned down
petitions signed by more than
$4,000 persons. >


Mrs. Ellis at her trial ad-I
mitted tracking her lover, 25-I
year-old David Blakely, to a
London bar and pumping four
bullets into him. Claiming her
jealousy had disturbed her emo
tions, she tried to get the murder
charge reduced to manslaughter.
The court threw out that de-
fense and jury Of 10 men and
2 women found her guilty on
June 81. after only "a minutes
of deliberation.


Two Women See Execution


Only government and prison
officials witnessed the execution
today. Two of them were
women: DR.. Charity Taylor, the
39-year-old governor of the
prison, and the prison matron.


More than 80 policemen,
standing shoulder to shoulder,
kept the crowd outside away
from the massive oak gates into
the prison yard. Just before the
execution Mrs. Ellis brother,
Julian Arthur Nelson, strobe
up to the gates. beat on them,
and handed bunch of white
carnations to a guard.


Returning to the crowd, his
face ashen and his lips trem-
bling, he said, II just told him
to tell Ruth I would never for
get her and God bless her."

Russia's new disarmament plan

West but falls far short Of what
the world needs, in the eyes Of
United States officials.


One vital element is missing
from the plan, those officials
say-an effective control on
arms production. The Russians
still do not accept allied de-
mands that a strong control
organization with inspection
powers be set up in order to
make sure that disarmament
pledges are met.


officials here are also dis
turbed by the manner in which
the Russians issued their plan.
1t was brought before the Lon
don Disarmament Conference
without warning. Soviet Dele
gate Jacob Malik read its en-
tire II pages in Russian with
out providing English or French
translationS, and Radio Mos
COW Immediately trumpeted the
story around the world.


May Become Key Issue


This technique, along with
the fact that the plan was
broached on the day the Big
Three invitation was issued to
Russia for a top level four-power
conference, causes fear that
propaganda may be an impor-
tant - and perhaps the para
mount-element in the new pro-
poSal.


Nevertheless, the fact that the
Russians have comeAup with a
plan that offers some compro-
mise with Western proposals has
prompted the State Department
to announce that it is getting
responsible consideration"


For one thing, the Russians
have accepted the Western idea
that armed forces should be
limited to specific figures rather
than cut 80 per cent across-the-
board as Russia has heretofore
proposed.


Modify Atom Arms Ban


Also, the Soviets agreed with
the allied plan Of last April 19
to bar atomic weapons at the
time that a proposed reduction
in conventional weapons is COM
pleted. In the past Russia want
ed this done after half the con-
ventional weapons cut had been
made.


Finally Russia has accepted
the idea of a single armament
control organization rather than
two. and dropped its insiStence
that this group be set up when
arms reductions begin. The
West wants the control unit set
up beforehand.

Republican Senator (then Rep
resentative) George H. Bender Of
Ohio said in January, 1854, that:
I'VE have eliminated more than
1000 Communists and fellow
travellers from important positions
in the Government Of the United
States. Every one Of these jobs was
obtained under the Democratic adj
ministration.


This was one of the early state
ments - really misstatements - on
security risks hat developed into
the number game" debate over
the COP cleanup Of the Federal
government. 1t. and other similar
announcements by Republicans
from the President on down, were
criticized by Democrats as distor-
tions of the facts.


Newsmen quickly found that few
of the persons removed had been
in important positions" and that
many had been only transferred.
not eliminated" But the other
allegations typified by the Bender
statement were harder to pin down.


Last week, however, Senate
subcommittee investigation showed
pretty much what the real story
was on security risk firings. The
Star commented editorially on
the findings:


Some Republican politicians
have grossly misrepresented the ex-
tent to which the Eisenhower adj
ministration has ferreted out Sc
curity risks in the Federal family"


The number in the numbers game
(Which once had been as great as
8,008) had settled down last week
to be 1886 (the number of removals
since the Eisenhower security pro-
gram went into effect May %.
1889, but administration witnesses
revealed that only a relatively
small number of those f1rings were
effected under the security pro-
gram. The commiCse majority
said the number was $40. The rest
were routine Civil Service
disiniSsals.


And the committee said also that
70 to rs per cent of the persons
fired had originally been hired by
the Eisenhower administration.


In other words, the Bender state
ment, which had neatly wrapped
up all the Republican errors on the
numbers game. was wrong in all its
important elements.

ANNAPOLIS, Feb. 26.-Navy
salvaged a winning season for
Coach Ben Carnevale today by
overcoming a woeful first half
with a phenomenal shooting ex-
hibition in the second to beat
Army. 67-45, before a Dahlgren
Hall crowd of 5000.


The Middies were five points
behind at halftime, 24-19. but
took the lead at 1928 five min
utes after intermission on Ken
McCally's side-court shot and
went on to win easily in a COM
plete turnabout performance.


The victory gave Carnevale
his ninth straight winning sea-
son and a To record in the Army
series. The Middies finished with
II victories against nine defeats
while Army ended at 10-all. In
the overall Army series. Navy
squared 1t with Is victories
apiece.

Army had slowed Navy with
a zone defense in the first half
with the Middies sticking to a
man-for-man. But Navy came
out with a zone in the. second
that completely befuddled the
Cadets. and for the last IS or
more minutes Army seldom got
a shot away that wasn't rushed,
or from way out.


Nays shooting average in the
first half was 26 per cent, it's
poorest of the season, but in the
second Navy hit for a phenome-
nal Sc per cent, its best. Both
Andy Dulik and Dave Smalley
made half their shots and tied
for scoring honors with Is points.


McCally, one of three Navy
regulars playing their last game.
was the fellow who broke the
ball game open.

came back with another, drove
all the way for a third straight

vet for a layup, and then hit
from the circle.

time-out and the Cadets never
were in the ball game after that.


Mark Binstein, who inspired
Army's upset over Navy last year,
was the key man in Army's Of

zone. He made only three points

and John Mcdonnell are the

officials in those countries. The Climate"

ABOARD AMPHIBIOUS FLAG
SHIP ESTES OFF TACHENS,
Feb. 12.-The rats took over the
Tachens today. The twin islands
200 miles north of Formosa are
all theirs until the Communists
come.


Rats-thousands of them, and
some as long as your forearm,
scurried through the deserted
villages as the last evacuation
ship pulled away from the mud
flats.


More than $4,000 Chinese
Nationalist troops and civilians
were removed in six days of
evacuation under the protective
guns, ships and planes of the
United States 7th Fleet.


Except for the rats, the islands
lie deserted-low, brown and
scrubby. The scene of teeming
activity week ago and frenzy
of loading operation for six days
now appeared like a medieval
area where the entire popula-
ton had packed and fled from
plague.


Village in Ruins.
Gone were the young and the
aged, the sick and the able, the
defended and the defenders. Big
Sun Hat village. pirates lair
in bygone centuries, lay smok-
ing in ruins today.


Fires started by bone-chilled
soldiers, waiting their turn to
board the ships, had spread to
the village and others. Many OF
the stone houses are burned out
hulks.


Elsewhere there are gaping
holes in the ground, where Ma
tionalist soldiers blasted their
elaborate Notifications. Explo-
sions shook the north island
every few minutes during the
early morning hours today.
showering colored flames and
rocking the ships of shore.


Eerie Silence Ensues.


BY daybreak the billowing ex-
plosions had ceased and an eerie
silence fell over the island. Sea
birds dipped low over the is
land. The brown waters Tapped
at a few small, leaky fishing
craft left behind with no one to
man them.


The early morning tide ebbed
for the first time in many cen
turies with no fishermen sailing
with it in search of food.
No heavy incense burned in
the Tachen temples. No house
wives haggled with merchants
at the markets. No one was born
there today. No one died. No
one laughed. No one cried. The
people of the Tachens had left
the home of their ancestors.


The islands lie dead and ST.
lent in sharp wintry wind.

A Senate subcommittee on juvenile
delinquency, after second look at condi-
tionS in Washington, has reported that
there is still room for improvement In the
handling of the youth-in-crime problem
here. The finding will occasion little surprise
among agencies charged with dealing with
the problem. There has been some change
for the better, however, since the subcom-
mittee first held hearings here more than
year ago. Any gain in this difficult field Is
welcome.


In its interim report last year the sub
committee severely criticized the lack OF
teamwork among such agencies as the
Juvenile Court, the Police Department and
the Welfare Department. The criticism was
thoroughly justified. Since then-and at
least partly because Of the senatorial re-
proach-there have been a number OF con-
ferences among the feuding officials, with
encouraging results. Both the Police Depart
ment and the Welfare Department now are
receiving information from the court which
previously had been difficult to obtain. And
the court is permitting the press to view
some of its operations, so that the public
is receiving more information about the
handling of delinquency cases before Judge
Cockrill'S tribunal.


The Police Department, too, has i'm
proved its organization for the more efficient
disposal of juvenile crime cases. A special
juvenile division under Inspector Winters
has taken over general supervision OF cases
involving teen-agers and other juveniles.
The new system seems to be working out
quite satisfactorily. AS the report pointed
out, however, Congress can assist local au-
thorities in meeting the wayward-youth
problem by providing more personnel and
funds for the court, the Police Department
and the Welfare Department. The subcom-
mittee's recommendations toward this end
should be of special interest to the Appro-
priations Committees of both houses.

The civil defense job was to or
ganize the operation and then 70
try out its communications system,
do a little small-scale evacuating
and then go through the motions
of caring for the injured and feed
ing and housing the evacuees.


There were snarls in each oper-
lion. naturally, but 1t was for the
purpose of spotting potential bugs
that the whole project was at
tempted.


Communication was basically
sound, although reports often were
delayed in transmission for hours.
and some messages never got there.
The theoretical relief operations
supposedly were effective, although
the actual reserves Of food, med
ical supplies and trained personnel
were present mostly on paper.


Civil defense people did profit in
two important ways: They found
the holes in their own organization,
and they put their story dramat-
ically across to thousands of per-
sons who count-Federal, State and
local authorities. It is those per-
sons whom civil defense must rely
on for support in improving the
program.

More than a m onth ago the
United States Public Health Sefv-
ices said the new Salk polio vaccine
was safe and effective. and 1t was
licensed for production.


BY the end of April the inocula-
ton program had started. but a
few children came down with polio
after receiving the shots-particu-
larly vaccine from one company,
Cutter Laboratories. The Public
Health Service said all the vaccine
was safe. but ordered the Cutter
supply withheld from the market.


Polio cases continued to crop up
in small numbers among vaccinated
children. The Public Health Service,
in the person of DR.. Leonard A.
Scheele, Surgeon General, said the
vaccine was entirely safe. Then he
ordered the vaccination program
suspended.


Rechecks of manufacturing and
testing methods were ordered. DR..
Scheele said the vaccine was safe.
He released one million-shot batch
for use, then, last week, another
378,000-dose shipment.


The next word was that all vac
cine manufactured was safe but
that no more would be released un-
til further notice-even from two
companies where a double check
had been completed.


Still Sofe, but


AS last week ended, the vaccine
was still officially safe, but it was
anybodys guess when vaccinations
would be resumed or whether the
two-shot series could be given the
5-through-9 age group before the
height Of the polio season late this
summer. Consensus of experts is
that while the second shot may be
administered at any time, the first
shot should not be given in polio
season.


The public was confused. DR..
Scheele: his boss. Mrs. Oveta Culp
Hobby, Secretary Of Health, Educa-
tion and Welfare; the President, and
physicians working in the vaccina-
ton program also seemed puzzled.


Apparently the manufacture and
use of the vaccine was going as
planned-when it was going. Yet
not all the results were as planned.
Effects of the Cutter vaccine were
"erratic." And no one could figure
out why.


Some 80 youngsters had contracted
polio after shots. Most had the
Cutter vaccine. Yet youngsters shot
from the same vial of Cutter vac
cine with the same needle and by
the same doctor as youngsters who
did catch polio, did not catch it.
And the Cutter product tested out
as safe, sound and effective.


Restudy, Recheck, Re-exomine


The Public Health Service seeme@
to think the only thing to do is
restudy, recheck and re-examine.


DR.. Jonas Salk himself said the
polio cases were clearly coinci-
dental" The vaccine was never
announced as 100 per cent effective.
he pointed out. but people seemed
to expect it to be.


Meanwhile Mrs. Hobby finished
work on suggested program of VOL
untary controls on distribution of
the vaccine. She suggested the
5-through-9 age group be shot first,
then the under-5 group, then the
10-through-19 youngsters, and f.
nally pregnant women. by then
whenever that may be-there should
be plenty for everybody. States and
medical societies would police the
priority program.


Mrs. Hobby was promptly blasted
by Senate Democrats for the late
ness and weakness of her plan. She
startled her critics by saying, '"No
one could have foreseen the public
demand for the vaccine"


Democrats shouted a fabber-
gasted "What?" They lashed her
for gross incompetence" and de-
manded her scalp. The President,
however. insisted she had done a
magnificent" job. But he added
that she had been planning for sew
eral months to retire because of the
i'll health Of her husband.

Things are bad, what with hurricanes,
the heat, the Communists and hay fever.
But they are not all bad, as witness the
case of Blackie, the cocker spaniel, in
nearby Edmonston, Maryland All is not
wrong with the world when men
notorious for their inhumanity to men
can devote hours of sweat and toll to the
rescue from a storm sewer Of trapped
dog. Blackie needed but to make his
plight known to passersby to get action.
Things soon began to buzz in Edmonston.
Firemen, policemen, plain citizens and
others tried various schemes for getting
the dog out, in vain. There was only one
way left-the hard way. Would the high
way authorities co-operate? They would
and did, without hesitation. So men with
picks and shovels and air drills went to
work digging up perfectly good street,
while traffic stopped and bystanders
cheered. It cost Maryland's taxpayers
$3.50 to retrieve Blackie from the sewer.

New personalities in big-power
diplomacy, dominant among them
President Eisenhower, produced an
unexpected result in the historic,
six-day meeting at the summit"
that ended yesterday at Geneva.


In one daring maneuver the
American President threw his cold
war adversary. the Soviet Union, on
the psychological defensive. This
in itself was almost wholly unfore-
seen before the conference began.


But more important. Mr.. Eisen-
hover set the world stage not for
a truce In the cold war, which was
what the Soviet Union wanted, but
for an eventual free world victory
without World War III. His British
and French colleagues, astounded
and perhaps skeptical. nevertheless
warmly endorsed his new effort.


Whether the President has the
intention to follow up his half
planned, half-spontaneous FIRST
step" at Geneva with co-ordinat-
ed executive and legislative effort
at home remains for the weeks and
months ahead to tell.


As for the formal business Of the
conference-German unity, Euro
pean security, disarmament. and
expansion of East-West contacts
nothing important was accom-
plished all week. The best the Big
Four could do was agree to try
again in the fall, with last weeks
smiles. instead Of the last decades
frowns, frozen on their faces.


Foreign ministers are to meet on
the German unity and European
security questions next October.
after the Soviet Union has had BIZ
lateral talks with NATO -allied West
Germany on the same subjects.


The United Nations disarmament
committee will resume its meetings
in New York August 20.

ant said one of the motorized

given for the troop movements.

Turkeys opposition to Syrian
alignment with Egypt and Saudi
Arabia in a proposed defense
alliance excluding non-Arab
members. Turkey has protested

Syrian relations have deterio-
rated rapidly the past few weeks.

Cornerstone Of the international
trade program is the Reciprocal
Trade Agreements Act, first passed
in 1884 and extended and modified
eight times. Under this act the
President can negotiate tariff ad-
justments with other nations in ex-
change for concessions to American
exports.


The measure expresses the "free
trade" philosophy Of the admins
tration: The more trade barriers are
broken down. the more American
and foreign economies will prosper.


On the other side are the pro
tectionists," who believe charity be-
gins at home, and who insist Amer
ican industries should be protected
from foreign sweat-shop competi-
ton.


Free Troders Prevail


Last weeks Senate votes on the
trade bill confirmed that free
traders far outnumber protection
lists in Congress. The Presidents
DILL, WIN lew amendments, passed,
rs to 13.


The House had passed a similar
measure, 295 to 10.


Two key amendments, added by
the Senate Finance Committee,
made concessions to protectionism.
One would permit the President to
set quotas on imports threatening
American industries vital to ma
tional defense. The other gave spe-
cial protection to textile manufac-
turers competing against Japanese
imports.


The expected flood Of special
amendments for other industries
particularly the oil industry-did
not materialize.

peasants In the neighborhood Of Gyoer.

have not barred the dispatch of news story
declaring that the recipients have been
made happy by the aid and feel very grate-

tarianism, for the moment at least, thus
seems to have punched a slight hole In the
wall that the Red totalitarians have erected
between their dark domain and the free
world, and nobody has been harmed by that
fact On the contrary, this little event, this
small contact between East and West, has
not merely brought succor to the hungry,
but has also served to illustrate how well
human beings can get along together, how
friendly and warn-hearted they can be,
when they are allowed to communicate with
one another instead Of being separated into
artificially hostile blocs created by the de-
vices Of tyranny # only the human touch
could be similarly applied everywhere behind
the Iron Curtain. mankind would soon be
rid OF the curse of the cold war and the way
would then be open for genuinely peaceful
coexistence.

food consumption is on the rise,
per capita farm income is NOV
ing up again and exports Of
some farm products are increas-
Ing.

machine has been producing at
an accelerated tempo since jan
uary. The Federal Reserve
Board reported that industrial
production in January averaged
100 per cent Of the 1947-1949 av-
erage. compared with 1913 per
cent in December and 124 per
cent o year ago. Last year the
January trend was downward.

The Washington Metropolitan Area.
after several years Of award-winning
traffic safety achievements, has had
regrettable and unaccountable setback.
Highway deaths during the past year
for the city and surrounding counties
have risen 81 per cent over 1854. And
the year is not over-indeed one of the
more dangerous periods Is right at hand.


According to American Automobile
Association figures 181 men, women and
children have been killed on public roads
in the Washington area SO far this year.
Last year-one that saw Washington and
several other communities setting COM
mendably low records-the total number
of traffic deaths was 112 Only two juriS-
dictionS have a better record this year
than last, Arlington and Prince Georges
Counties. All other areas have expert
enced a tragic upturn in serious auto
mobile accidents. Washington set rec
ord low mark for traffic fatalities last
year, when SO persons died as result
of street and highway accidents But
that figure was passed some time ago,
and in the middle of this month the
death toll stood at &c..


Until the local statistics are carefully
analysed, safety authorities will not know
the reason for the years bad record.
Certainly there was not any noticeable
letdown in traffic enforcement, engineer
ing or education, which are the so-called
three Els of safety" But the statistics
always have proved one thing: That it is
the human factor, not mechanical or
other factors, that is Of major Importance
in preventing accidents That is why the
AAA, the National Safety Council and
other authorities are trying to impress
drivers that their lives, as well as the
lives of others, are in their own hands.
The warnings are especially pertinent
during the holiday season, when driver
fatigue, driver carelessness, and drink
induced driver reckleSsnesS are usually
prevalent.

island chain off Red China since

stewardess, Sarah tKathy)
Reeves Of Dania, Fla. as the
heroine of the crash. She
opened the cabin door and
Gained the passengers as they
stepped from the plane.


The twin-engine Lockheed
Lodestar was taking of from
Pinellas International Airport
for Sarasota, Fort Myers and
West Palm Beach before reach
ing Miami. The flight originated
at Jacksonville.

runway, the planes landing gear
apparently collapsed and the
wing scraped ground. The right
engine then caught fire and
flames spread to the rest of the
plane.


There was no panic among
the passengers, who lost all their
luggage.


The plane was piloted by
Capt. Marshal Hope, 46, of
Miami. The co-pilot was George
Graham. 26, Hastings-on-H -Hud-
son. N. Y. Both are based at
Miami. Miss Reeves is based
at Jacksonville.


NAL said the crew was highly
commended" for its speedy work
in getting the passengers from
the plane before it caught fire.

COPENHAGEN, Norway. Feb
1.-Holger Nielsen, SO. retired
lieutenant colonel in the Danish
Army, who perfected the Mel
sen method of artificial respira-
ton which is used all over the
world, died yesterday.


The Nielsen method of artifi-
cial respiration supplanted the
Schaeffer or prone pressure
method in 1851. The operator
kneels facing the patient. instead
of astride his hips, and exerts
pressure on the shoulder blades
rather than the ribs. The pres
sure is completed by slight
raising of the patients arms,
thus taking the weight off the
chest and causing the lungs to
accept more air than could be
taken through other methods.

sion of the city's' nine main

stoppage, which also shut the
financial and sporting papers

mass meeting that the stoppage
probably would last into next
week.


Sports enthusiasts were with
out late word from their favorite
columnists on two of the nations
biggest sporting events, the
Grand National and the Oxford
Cambridge boat race, both
scheduled for today. w.

ing Corp. for news. There was

magazines.

not affected by the strike, but
none are being distributed in the
capital.


Labor and management met
with government Cancellation
officials last night @and later
strikers mass meetings were
called.


The unions want new pay
raises to meet the increased cost
of living, but they have not made
public what they are asking.

BARNES. England, Dec. 8 up
"A train packed with home
ward-bound theater-goers
crashed into a standing freight
train in this London suburb last
night and burst into a soaring
mass of flames. Thirteen persons
were burned to death and IS
others were injured.
Two Of the dead were young
children. Twenty-seven Of the
injured were reported in serious
condition today.


The electric train carrying $50
passengers from London's West
End to their homes in the
Thames Valley ripped into the
rear of the freight train just
outside Barnes Station. Barnes
is 8 miles west of Central Lon
don.


The first coach overturned and
dug a path along an embank-
ment before stopping. The COL
lision shorted the cars power
circuit. There was a moments
silence and then the crumpled
coach exploded into flames.
Screams Rise Above Roar


The screams of the trapped
and injured sounded above the
roar of the fire as dazed pas
sengers from the rear coaches
sought to give aid.


Railroad workers and unin-
jured passengers tore at the
wreckage with their bare hands.
They hurried the injured they
could remove to houses along
the tracks.


| The accident occurred below a
highway bridge. Firemen fought
the flames from 20 feet above
the wreck scene. The fire
melted the asphalt roadway
surface about the firemen and
heated the steel bridge Orders
to a glowing red.


George Peters, a 55-year -old
of duty railway engineer, was
riding in the third coach. He
said his one thought was to cut
of the electric current.

TAIPEH, Formosa, Feb. A.
Nationalist China's President
Chang Kai-shek was reported
today to be considering a United
States request that he evacuate
his troops from the Red-threat-
ened Tachen Islands, 200 miles
north of Formosa.


Responsible Government
spokesmen said fatty tonight
there was no truth in reports
that Gen. Chang had rejected
the request. They said no state
ment on the subject has yet
been made.


The request is believed to have
been transmitted by United
States Ambassador Karl I. Ran
kin Wednesday, who reportedly
pointed out that the mighty 7th
Fleet could not be held in readi-
ness indefinitely. 4


Red Rejection Hints Trouble.


Red China's bristling rejection
of a U. N. invitation to join in
cease-fire talks signaled trouble.
And there was increasing talk
at middle Nationalist levels of
fighting for the Tachens instead
of abandoning them to the Reds.


The Nationalists have long ac-
knowledged the ability of the
Communists to launch an am
phibiouS attack on the Tachens
at a moments notice. Right now,
however, no such attack appears
imminent.


] Nationalist planes pounded the
Reds hard last night, and the
Communists replied today with
a minor artillery barrage on
Quemoy Island.


The Nationalist Defense Min
istry said the Reds hurled IL
shells into Quemoy this after
noon from Tateng in Annoy Bay.
The Red guns fell silent when
Nationalist guns returned the
fire, the ministry said.


Chiang's Planes Blast Reds.


Gen. Chiang's warplanes
ranged the East China Sea
around the tense area last night,
bombing and shooting up Chinese
Communist shipping and the
newly-won Red base of Yiki-
angshan Island.


Official reports said the bomb
ers destroyed two vessels near
Nantien Island, 80 miles north
of the Tachens. scored hits on
two more about II miles north
east of the Tachens and bombed
nearby Yikiangshan with excel
lent results.


Another small American-built
transport landed today at the
north coast port of Keelung with
refugees from devasted Lower
Tachen. Aboard were Ill sick
and wounded Nationalist SOL
diers, 81 prisoners from Tachen
iails and 6 civilians.


Powerful 7th Fleet units
cruised off Formosa today.
primed for orders to evacuate
the 10000 troops and civilians
from the two Tachen Islands.
But the orders appeared stalled
in dispute between Gen. Chang
and the United States over the
fate of two other Nationalist
outposts, Quemoy and Matsu.

The uprisings last week weren't
pretty. The French had expected
trouble and concentrated their
army contingents in the big popu-
lation centerS. So the Moroccan
Nationalist did most of their dam
age in the countryside. In Oued
Fem, for instance, some 80 French
men. women and children were re-
ported killed by tribesn1en swoop-
ing down out of the mountains.
Few were allowed to die quickly.


BY midweek. Frances army was
conducting reprisal raids through
the Oued Fem district. rounding up
offenders and searching Moroccans
for weapons.


French colonS openly sought re-
venge. Friday French army officers
said that some $4,000 to 10000
tribesmen were surrendering in the
Atlas Mountains. At Oued Fem,
Gen. Antoine Franchi, military
governor in the area, assembled
thousands Of Moroccans and called
them Sinking jackals" for murder
ing French residents.


II have troops and artillery and
planes which can reduce everything
to dust" Gen. Franchi doomed into
the loud speakers. II am giving
you orders and if they are not
obeyed I will return, and this time
there will be no quarter"


He said French arms had been
stolen. and gave eight days for their
return. If they were not brought
back by then. he said, the whole
tribe would be punished.


Overhead French fighters flew
cover" and near the general stood
tanks with heavy guns.


Some sources specialized that the
uprisings had their roots in rivalries
between Arabs and Berbers. The
Berbers were the original inhabi-
tants Of Morocco. Arabs came
many hundreds Of years ago. Pro-
Moroccans contend, however. that
the Arab-Berber distinction no
longer applies. that the French have
played upon it TO divide and rule. "
They say that last weeks uprisings
by Berbers, who had supposedly
been led by the pro-French Pasha
of Marrakesh, confirm their claim
that Arabs and Berbers alike seek
more freedom and independence.

cost more lives (the Johnstown flood
Of 1889 was the worst, causing 1900
deaths). but probably none have
done as much property damage as
the floods which New England was
digging out Of last week.


The cost in lives was heavy, Of
course. Not all the bodies had been
found or the MISSING accounted for
as the week ended, but the toll ap-
parently was about 200 lives. There
was no way to measure the suffering
Of the survivors.


Property damage was estimated
at SIG billion. On top Of that will
be probably another billion dollars
in lost wages and lost production.
1t will be decades before the debt
Is paid.


How Waters Grew


The New England floods were the
product Of two hurricanes. Connie
swept up the Atlantic Seaboard
more than two weeks ago, carrying
with her tremendous quantities of
water. The rains swelled rivers
and creeks and saturated the
ground. Then another heavily laden
hurricane, Diane, followed roughly
the same path and dropped her rain
over the same area.


DANES deluge ran of the soaked
ground into the swollen creeks. The
Weather Bureau forecast floods OH
major rivers. and precautions were
taken. But the Weather Bureau
is small agency. and 1t could not
make detailed forecasts for the
streams and tributaries.


Flood waters rose almost without
warning in narrow valleys of New
England. Homes and factories
were inundated. Bridges, railroads
and highways were washed away.


Persons. including President
Eisenhower, who looked at the
damage were appalled,. Families,
homes and jobs were wiped out.
Fires were burning and the people
had no means to put them out.
Typhoid germs were everywhere,
in the mud that filled the houses
and In the water the people had
to boil and drink.


Mony Helping Honds


New Englanders went to work to
clean UP the mess. And the whole
world helped.


Emergency care for the homeless
and injured was the first job. The
Red Cross set out to raise So mil
lion. Contributions came in from
every State and from generous
foreign countries. Even the little
Dominican Republic gave 100000.
Washington, D. c.. was raising
$4,000.


Long-range rehabilitation will be
q more costly task. New England
States mortgaged their future in
comes. The Federal Government
cut through red tape and promised
billion dollars in aid, mostly from
Army Engineer funds. CKey Con-
gressmen said they would make up
the sum in next years appropria-
lions, though they could make no
formal commitment


Almost no one had flood insur-
ance. as IL is virtually impossible
to buy. So outside aid was i'm
perative.


1t was up to the men and women
on the scene. however, to do the
dirty work of digging out.


Thousands of homes were con-
demned. and they will be torn
down. People who owned them will
have to start saving all over again.


Most factory owners and bust
nessmen set about rebuilding. There
were some businesses. however,
that might never be reopened.
New Flight Of Industry?


New England was already in an
industrial pinch, with many fac
tories moving to the cheaper South.
Some businesses remained in New
England only because they had
paid-for factory buildings there.
They will hesitate to rebuild at
present prices on old sites.


Few New Englanders. however.
doubted their ability to recover
eventually from the onslaught of
Connie and Diane.


There was one somberly hopeful
note. Some of the towns hardest
hit planned to embark on moderni-
zation programs which they had
been putting off these many years.

ginia and West Virginia. and the

divided into five regular geo.
graphical Jurisdictions, and one

Jurisdiction.

area, a unit of the regular
Northeastern jurisdiction, was
taken under permissive legisla-
ton of the church's last general
conference, permitting such
transfers, but still must be ap-
proved by the overall jurisdic-
tions involved.


The conference was called by
Bishop Frederick Buckley Newell
of the New York area and Bishop
Edgar A. Love of the Baltimore
area. and represented 1000
churches with 100000 members.

If Government employees again fail to
obtain the pay raise which they have
sought so long, they should place the
blame where it properly belongs-on Con-
gress, not President Eisenhower. Congress,
for the second time, has ignored White
House warnings of possible veto of too
liberal pay legislation. And once more the
implied threat of presidential veto has
imperiled the chances of an increased pay
scale for all Federal workers.


The pay bill approved by the House,
by vote split largely along partisan lines,
has the virtue Of being less Objectionable
to the administration than the Senate
approved measure The House bill calls
for an average raise of 8.3 per cent for
postal workers, instead of the maximum
7.6 per cent which the President had
asked. The Senate had voted for 10 per
cent Increase figure certain to be vetoed
If submitted. The House measure Is bet
ter than the Senate version in another
important respect-it provides for read
justment Of postal salaries according to
nature and amount of work performed.
Postal unions have opposed tying the pay
raise and Redistribution together despite
administration insiStence that the two
subjects 60 hand in hand.


Since the President personally has
not stated publicly that any pay raise
higher than 7.6 per cent would be vetoed,
there remains for the employees the hope
that he might accept the House figure,
If 1t should emerge from the Senate-House
conference. But the economy minded ad-
ministration faces the fact that what Is
right for postal workers is right for all
Federal employees. And the House action
would add about $12 million to the cost
Of pay legislation for the postal workers
alone. The President and his advisers have
commended that the Government cannot
afford the cost of general raise higher
than 7.6 per cent. All Of this advice has
been shunted aside under much pressure
from the organized postal workers. If the
President should take strong veto stand,
there is considerable doubt that enough
votes could be marshaled to override it..
Thus, the present outlook for an early pay
raise is clouded with uncertainty, to say
the least.

The land Is blowing again In the
Southern Great Plains.


Over 40 million acres are reported
"ready to blow" in huge area CEN
tered around the old "dust bowl" of
the 1930s. If conditions are right"
this spring. the Nation will again be
seeing the sun through brown haze
from Denver eastward to the Allan
tic seaboard, and thousands Of farm
ers in Kansas, Texas, Oklahoma, Ne
braska, Colorado and New Mexico
will see their farms whisked away
and their livelihood destroyed.


"H conditions are right" the ex-
perts say. Land blows every year in
that immense prairieland where dry
winds almost never cease and where
the topsoil for the most part is thin.
But only the right" conditions can
bring about the vast blowing that
was the disaster OF the middle and
late sos.


So far this year, conditions are
just too right. There have been sew
eral dry years, crop seasons too poor
to permit the successful growth Of
substantial cover on the loose, pow
dery soil. Since the autumn har-
vests, rain and snow fall has been
below normal. And the winds have
been stronger. -Four million acres
were reported seriously damaged by
blowing this winter, with the high
winds Of December doing most Of
the destruction. January was some
what better, the Agriculture Depart
ment says, but the real high-wind
months are still ahead. II the
drought continues, and the March
and April winds are even normally
strong. the prospects are ominous.


AS last week ended heavy SHOWS
were falling in some sections Of
the drought-stricken plains area.
Though some news reporters pro-
claimed that the drought was
broken" it seemed probable that
it would take a couple Of wet years
not just few wet days-to put
an end to the dust-producing con-
ditions now periling the Midwest.
Chronic Drought


Drought in the Great Plains is
no rare phenomenon. Next to the
ever-present winds, drought is prob
ably the most dependable feature Of
the climate. The prolonged dry
spell of the '30s was the worst since
weather records were started, but
drought In varying degrees Of in
tensity has probably been feature
of the Plains for centuries. The
great dryness comes in cycles, but
the cycles are not of any regular
pattern that would permit of reason
ably accurate prediction.


When the great, fiat stretches Of
prairieland knew only the hooves Of
buffalo and Indian ponies, there
were no dust storms. A tough cover
of wild grasses held down the light
topsoil while it gave sustenance to
the buffalo and thence to the Indian.
But the white man pushed West to
follow his manifest destiny, and
where the white man went, there
went the pillow.


Homesteaders poured into the
Great Plains in the years between
1870 and 1890, built their sod shacks
and plowed UP the prairie grass. For
a few years crops were good. the
virgin soil producing copiously with
the aid Of good rains and relatively
moderate winters.


Rut In 1890 the growing season
was dry, and the dryness continued
through 1894-the first disaster in
the region following its initial cul-
tivation. Thousands Of settlers went
back East, leaving their farms to
the winds and the coyotes. BY 1894
the population Of many Western
Kansas counties was less than 1t had

port on its study of youth prob
lens.

sary nor economically sound,

linquents than Prince Georges

regulations so that persons with

from driving cabs in the county.

49, Last week Germany cleared its

peanized"-neither country would

nently out of the Adenauer coalition.

itself was torn internally when Vice

Democratic leader, stuck with

The strife within the coalition
and within the Free Democratic
Party will make it more difficult for
the Adenauer government to oper-
ate in the future Though the
chancellor still would have ma
jority in Parliament without the

that Herr Adenauer was unlikely to
let Herr Bleucher resign, and it also

ocrats would GUST him from the

an uneasy continuation of the old
coalition.

The workable program" submitted to
the Commissioners by team Of consultants
might well form the battle plan for an
effective ten-year attack on urban blight
In the Nations Capital. The campaign
already has begun in the Southwest section,
where drastic slum- clearance and redevel
opment methods are being used. There are
sore spots elsewhere which need similar
treatment. But there also are other large
areas where renewal and renovation proc
esses, undertaken jointly by public and
private enterprise, can accomplish wonders
once community sentiment demands
action. The experts report points the way
for such co-ordinated campaign


Federal cooperation in such broad
undertaking has been promised under the
1854 Housing Act, provided the District
adopts workable program" for gradual
elimination Of Slums and rundown districts
generally. Formal approval, therefore, Of
some such plan of campaign as that rec
commended by the consultants is pre-
requisite to Federal participation in further
District warfare on slums and other mani
festations Of city decay. Some Of the areas
designated In the report for rebuilding or
renewal already have been earmarked for
improvement. These include, In additioa to
the Southwest. the downtown Northwest
section chosen by the National Capital
Planning Commission and the Redevelop-
ment Land Agency for an urban renewal"
project, and Marshall Heights and Barry
Farms in the eastern section of the city,
where first attempts at redevelopment were
frustrated by neighborhood protests and
congressional disapproval. The report adds
number Of fringe spots in the older parts
of the Northwest for future rehabilitation.


The broad fight outlined by the experts
would involve co-ordinated teamwork by
Federal District and private interests, with
the District government assuming leader
ship Of the drive. About two-thirds of the
ten-year aggregate public cost of $500, ,000,-
600 would be contributed from Federal funds
and the remainder by the District. But,
the consultantS said, all or most of the
District cost could be written of under the
new public works program In the form OF
street, sanitation and other public improve
ments already contemplated. And the Dis
trict would gain large additional tax rev.
enues from the restored areas. Private
interests would have to provide substantial
sums for new construction under redevelop-
ment plans and for renewal under strictly
enforced housing and zoning regulations.
The emphasis laid by the advisers on the
need for positive leadership to make the
workable program actually work is justified.
Without such leadership at the District
government level. abetted by community
and congressional support. much of the
program is apt to remain on paper.

NEW YORK, June A. Auto
production dropped this week to
its lowest level of the year. but
activity in most other lines held
close to record peaks.


Things still hummed in such
key areas Of the economy as steel
production. coal mining. heavy
construction. rail freight trafic
and electric energy consumption.


Businessmen sizing UP the OUT
look for the summer had plenty
Of reason for optimism. Some
showdown in overall activity was
inevitable, many felt, but the dip
would be q mild one, and 1t
wouldn't last long.


The trend was apparent in the
nations basic industry, steel.
Mills. going full blast at nearly
|s7 per cent of capacity. were
still unable to keep pace with
the flood Of new orders; some
would soon shut down for long
overdue repairs.


Cutbacks In auto production
reflected sporadic walkouts and
the Memorial Day holiday. but
1t was evident that most Of the
automakers would have slashed
their output anyway.


The retail trade remained on
q high plateau. Department
store sales for the week ended
May 20 were 10 per cent higher
than in the comparable week Of
1854; total retail sales for the
week through Wednesday. DUN
& Bradstreet said. ranged from 4
to 8 per cent higher than q year
ago.


Total retail volume for June
was headed for the $15.5 billion
mark, an all-time record for the
month.

running the city during fiscal 1856 is in

ment expenses, fire protection, and SANTA
ton. These items lead the list of operating

categories as the foregoing especially at
time when all Of them are clamoring for

omy opportunities among the remaining
agencies, but since their total budget repre-

The atomic submarine Maui
titus will head out to sea soon
to test her speed and stealth
against the best of the Nays
anti-submarine forces on a
"shakedown" cruise of thou
sands of miles.


The 3.000-ton nuclear subma-
rine came back into New Lon
don. Conn, late last week from
a demonstration and test con-
Quoted for Navy Survey Board
which approves new ships.


Logs 5000 Miles


The Nautilus crew already has
sailed her more than 5000 miles
and dived almost 100 times. But
most of this has been to test
her mechanical performance for
the Electric Boat Division of
General Dynamics Corp, which
built her, and for study by Navy
technicians.


The normal shakedown cruise
for a conventional submarine
lasts between two and four
weeks, but, it was learned, that
of the Nautilus will extend far
longer and over much greater
distances. There was no in
dication. however, that this first
real sea cruise would be a test
of the claimed round-world
cruising capability of the first
atomic submarine. Such
demonstration may come later.


The probability is that the
Nautilus will cruise in the West
ern Atlantic and Caribbean.
For the first time. she will travel
without the mothering attention
of a submarine rescue vessel
which has accompanied her on
most trips up to now.


To Test Evasion Powers


The tactical phase of the
shakedown cruise will test out
the Nautilus escape and evasion
capabilities. She can dive much
deeper and go much faster than
any conventional submarine. The
Nautilus probably will work
against destroyer escorts, planes
and blimps which are equipped
with the most modern detection

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina,
May 20 (Pl.-Argentina's Peron-
dominated Chamber of Deputies
gave overwhelming approval last
night to the presidents demand
to end Roman Catholicism as the
state religion.


In the first formal step toward
amending the constitution, the
lower house voted 121-12 for the
government backed proposal to
eliminate Catholicism favored
legal position. The bill calls
for election of national con-
vention to change the nations
basic law,


Victory in the lower chamber
has been certain. The Peronista
Party normally controls 149 of
the 166 seats. TheIbill now goes
to the Senate-where Peronistas
hold all 81 seats-and then to
the president for signature.
ing two days of debate on the
isue. wound up with boisterous
demonstrations both in the
chamber and outside.


Catholic Youths Parade


Deputies pounded on their
desks and shouted "Peron!
Peron!" Outside several hundred
Catholic youths paraded toward
the capitol, chorusing "Argen-
tina is Catholic" and Long live
Christ the King" until police dis
persed them.


Earlier in the evening thou
sands of Catholics packed the
metropolitan cathedral and 70
other churches in Buenos Aires
for evening masses. Officially
they marked observance of the
Feast of the Ascension. But the
unusual number of evening
masses made apparent the
church authorities intended a
demonstration of support.


Police stationed heavy con-
centrations near the principal
churches, but the marching
youths were the only demon
strators.


After Senate action and Gen.
Peron's signature on the bill, the
government will call an election
for the assembly to reWrite the
constitution. The vote is expected
late this year.


Effects of Action


Removal from the constitution
of references to the church would
spell the end of all financial aid
to church schools and discon-
tinuance of the small salaries
paid from government funds to
cardinals, bishops and other
churchmen.


The Senate already has passed
q bill canceling the tax exemption
of churches and religious bodies.
The measure was scheduled for
debate in the deputies chamber
today


Both House and Senate also
have approved a bill to end Cath
olic religious education in public
schools.


Gen. Peron has been carrying
on an open battle with the church
In this mainly Catholic country
since last November. The presi-
dent has accused some members
of the clergy of seeking to under
mine his regime. Since Novem-
ber. Al priests have been arrested.
but many were later released.


The church has denied the gov
ernment charges and Vatican
organs have accused Gen. Peron
of dictatorial tactics.
